question: Deaf children in Nicaragua, brought together in new schools in the 1980s, did what with their improvised signs?
options: Turned them into a full new language
answer: They built a full sign language, with grammar richer than the gestures they started with, and the youngest children used it most fluently. Pinker tells the story as near-direct evidence of the instinct: children do not just learn a language, they can create one.
move: Given each other, children don't only learn language: they invent it.
trap: 'Kept simple gestures': without teachers, nothing complex seems possible.
simply: A group of kids with no shared language made up their own, with real grammar, and the youngest spoke it best. That's how strong the language instinct is.
why: It is a rare look at a language being born, and a reminder of what young brains can do when they share a need to talk.

book.title: The Language Instinct
book.author: Steven Pinker
book.badge: By a two-time Pulitzer Prize finalist

reference: Steven Pinker, The Language Instinct (William Morrow, 1994), ch. 2
